summary: Specifies three tools needed for debugging networks that use CLNP: a ping or OSI Echo function, a traceroute that uses that echo, and a routing table dump.

plainLanguage.summary: If a message gets lost, you need ways to ask, are you there, and which way did it go. This memo describes those tools for one network type.

questions: what tools are required for clns
subtitle: The minimum debugging toolkit for CLNP networks: ping, traceroute and a routing table dump.

tldr.problem: As OSI protocols spread across the Internet, network-layer debugging tools were almost nonexistent, and the ones that existed did not interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The memo requires every CLNP host and router to support an echo function (ping), a traceroute that uses the ISO 8473 Lifetime field, a routing table dump, SNMP access to two CLNS MIB tables, and a common osi host.txt name-to-NSAP file format.
tldr.outcome: It is the baseline support level for CLNS hosts and routers. It is Informational and obsoletes RFC 1139.

today: RFC 1574 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1139. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why a Minimum Toolkit
sections.content:
RFC 1574 notes that OSI protocols were being used more and more in an Internet that was once mostly TCP/IP. Network managers found that network layer OSI debugging tools were almost nonexistent, and when they existed, different implementations did not work together.

The memo defines the minimum subset of tools needed to debug problems in networks using ISO 8473 (CLNP, the connectionless network protocol): ping, traceroute and a routing table dump. It says these mechanisms MUST be available on every router (intermediate system) and every host (end system) that provides OSI service. It relies on the echo mechanism of RFC 1575 and obsoletes RFC 1139.
sections.plainLanguage: Different brands of OSI computers could not even check on each other when something broke. This paper sets the smallest set of tools everyone must have.

sections.title: Ping and the OSI Echo Function
sections.content:
Ping uses the echo mechanism of RFC 1575, which needs two new type values in the ISO 8473 packet header: 1E (hex) for the echo-request selector and 1F (hex) for the echo-response selector. All hosts and routers MUST support the echo function and MUST also set the ERROR report flag in the header.

The error flag matters because it lets a compliant node ping a non-compliant one. A node that does not understand the new type MUST try to return an ISO 8473 error packet, which still shows that it is reachable. A ping utility MUST report the round trip time of each packet plus the average, minimum and maximum over several packets, and MUST report the error code when an error packet comes back.
sections.plainLanguage: Ping is shouting 'are you there?' and timing the echo. If the other side does not know the game, it still has to shout back 'I do not understand', which also proves it is there.

sections.title: Traceroute with the Lifetime Field
sections.content:
CLNP trace works like ping but uses the Lifetime field, which serves the same purpose as the Time To Live field in an IP packet. A node cannot forward a packet whose Lifetime is zero. The sender sends echo-requests with Lifetime 1, then 2, and so on, and each hop that runs the value down returns an error packet that reveals its identity.

A node that supports echo returns A0 (Lifetime expired in transit) or A1 (expired during reassembly). A node that does not support echo-request returns B0 (unsupported option not specified). The trace ends when the destination answers, or when it receives B0, 80 (destination address unreachable) or 81 (destination address unknown).

For a defined list of other error codes, such as 00 to 07, B1 to B4 and C0, the sender should send a second packet. Optional partial source routeing allows a third-party trace, and errors 92 and 93 then terminate the trace. A traceroute utility should show the Network Entity Title of each system on the path, round trip times, error codes and other errors.
sections.plainLanguage: Send a note that expires after one stop, then two stops, then three. Each stop that sees the note expire tells you who it is, so you learn the whole path.

sections.title: Routing Table Dump and SNMP
sections.content:
Each OSI host or router MUST be able to dump any of its routing tables, whether learned from ES-IS, static configuration, IS-IS, IDRP or another source, through some out-of-band mechanism. A show osi routes command SHOULD exist with options a, esis, isis, idrp, static and other. Routing tables SHOULD also be available through SNMP or CMIP.

Two objects from the CLNS MIB of RFC 1238 are named for SNMP: clnpAddrTable (addresses for interfaces) and clnpRoutingTable (OSI routes in the system routing table). The memo says that RFC remains the authoritative source for the definitions, and that not everything needed is in the CLNS MIB, so more MIB work was expected.
sections.plainLanguage: Every OSI machine must be able to show you its map when you ask, and also hand it over to monitoring software.

sections.title: The OSI host.txt Format
sections.content:
OSI addresses (NSAPs) can be 20 bytes. In the long term DNS or the OSI Directory (X.500) would map names to addresses, but in practice each system used a fixed table and every implementation used a different format. The memo defines one fixed format so these files can be shared.

Each line is <NSAP Address> <name1> <name2> .... The address octets are in hexadecimal. Dots are only aids to reading, MUST NOT be required for parsing, and implementations MUST handle their insertion anywhere. The mapping MUST be available to ping, traceroute and CLNS routing table look-up. Hosts and routers MUST also support NSAP-to-name mapping through DNS or X.500.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a shared address book where each line has a long number and the friendly names for that machine. Everyone uses the same layout so books can be swapped.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says only that security issues are not discussed. It adds no authentication or protection for the echo, traceroute or table-dump functions.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors did not talk about keeping bad guys out in this paper.
